```lean
theorem evolveHalfLeft_eq_column (X : Config) (t k : ℕ) :
    evolveHalfLeft (column X 0) (fun k => X (-((k : ℤ) + 1))) t k
      = column X (-((k : ℤ) + 1)) t :=
```

Description: The left half of the picture, the cells at x ≤ -1, is driven by the centre column alone: a cell there reads its two neighbours and itself, all at x ≤ 0, and the one at x = 0 is the centre column. This node says the half-line model in Basic.lean is exactly that half of any picture, for every row and every time. It is the definition that lets a theorist or a prover talk about the left half with the centre column as a free parameter instead of a consequence, which is the move Sextant's second attack turned on. Proof: induction on t generalising k; each cell is one rule30_eq; the k = 0 case reads column X 0 t, which is definitionally evolveFrom X t 0. On the cast warning: the ℤ here is a position, not a count. column is indexed by ℤ and the cells left of the origin sit at negative positions, so no ℕ form of the statement exists; the only cast arithmetic a prover meets is -((k + 1 : ℕ) : ℤ) = -(k : ℤ) - 1 and its like, which push_cast (or omega on the index) closes in one line.. 3	
4	An *elementary cellular automaton* is about as small as a dynamical system
5	gets: a bi-infinite row of black/white cells, updated in lock-step by a rule
6	that looks only at each cell and its two neighbours.
7	
8	This file defines all 256 of them from a rule number, specialises to rule 30,
9	and proves the one bridging lemma (`rule30_eq`) that every downstream proof
10	uses.
11	-/
12	import Mathlib.Data.Int.Notation
13	import Mathlib.Logic.Function.Iterate
14	import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Card
15	import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Pi
16	import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Card
17	
18	/-- A configuration of the automaton: a bi-infinite row of cells, each black
19	(`true`) or white (`false`), indexed by the integers.
20	
21	In TypeScript terms this is exactly `(i: bigint) => boolean`. There is no
22	array, no bound, and no "edge of the world" — the row really is the function.
23	-/
24	abbrev Config : Type := ℤ → Bool
25	
26	namespace ElementaryCA
27	
28	/-- The neighbourhood of a cell, packed into the 3-bit number Wolfram numbers
29	his rules by: `left` is the high bit (4), `center` the middle bit (2), `right`
30	the low bit (1). So the all-black neighbourhood `111` is index `7`, and the
31	all-white one `000` is index `0`.
32	
33	`Bool.toNat` is the obvious `false ↦ 0`, `true ↦ 1`. -/
34	def neighborhoodIndex (left center right : Bool) : Nat :=
35	  4 * left.toNat + 2 * center.toNat + right.toNat
36	
37	/-- One step of the elementary cellular automaton with rule number `r`.
38	
39	A rule number *is* its own lookup table. Three neighbours give 8 possible
40	neighbourhoods, and the rule must supply one output bit for each — so a rule is
41	exactly one byte, and `Fin 256` is that byte. `Fin 256` carries the proof of
42	its own bound with it, so `step 300` is not a runtime error, it is unwritable.
43	
44	`Nat.testBit r.val k` reads bit `k` of the rule number, which is the output for
45	neighbourhood `k`. -/
46	def step (r : Fin 256) (c : Config) (i : ℤ) : Bool :=
47	  r.val.testBit (neighborhoodIndex (c (i - 1)) (c i) (c (i + 1)))
48	
49	end ElementaryCA
50	
51	/-- Rule 30, the automaton the Wolfram prizes are about.
52	
53	This is a *partial application*, not a wrapper: `ElementaryCA.step` takes a rule
54	first, so `ElementaryCA.step 30` is already a value of type `Config → Config`.
55	(Every Lean function takes exactly one argument, so there is no such thing as
56	"calling `step` with a missing argument" — currying is not opt-in here.) -/
57	def rule30 : Config → Config := ElementaryCA.step 30
58	
59	/-- The initial configuration the prize questions are stated against: a single
60	black cell at the origin on an infinite white background.
61	
62	`decide (i = 0)` turns the *proposition* `i = 0` into the `Bool` that says
63	whether it holds; the two are different things in Lean, and only the `Bool` can
64	be stored in a cell. -/
65	def initialConfig : Config := fun i => decide (i = 0)
66	
67	/-- The configuration after `t` steps of rule 30, starting from
68	`initialConfig`.
69	
70	`f^[t]` is `Nat.iterate`: `f` composed with itself `t` times. `rule30^[0]` is
71	the identity, so `evolve 0 = initialConfig`. -/
72	def evolve (t : Nat) : Config := rule30^[t] initialConfig
73	
74	/-- The center column: the colour of the origin cell after `t` steps.
75	
76	This single sequence of bits is the subject of all three Rule 30 Prize
77	questions (see `Rule30/Prize.lean`). It is OEIS A051023. -/
78	def centerColumn (t : Nat) : Bool := evolve t 0
79	
80	/-- The `k`-th diagonal in from the **left** edge of the cone, read `j` steps
81	along it: the cell at position `-j` after `j + k` steps. `leftDiagonal 0` is
82	the left edge itself, `leftDiagonal 1` the cells just inside it, and so on.
83	
84	In TypeScript terms it is a re-indexing, `(k, j) => evolve(j + k)(-j)`, and
85	nothing more — no new data, only a coordinate system in which the left side
86	of the pattern reads as a family of one-dimensional sequences. -/
87	def leftDiagonal (k j : Nat) : Bool := evolve (j + k) (-(j : ℤ))
88	
89	/-- The `k`-th diagonal in from the **right** edge, read `j` steps along it:
90	the cell at position `j` after `j + k` steps. Not the mirror image of
91	`leftDiagonal`: rule 30 is not left-right symmetric, and the two families
92	behave differently. -/
93	def rightDiagonal (k j : Nat) : Bool := evolve (j + k) (j : ℤ)
94	
95	/-- `f` repeats with period `p` from index `N` on: `f (n + p) = f n` for every
96	`n ≥ N`. The prefix before `N` is unconstrained.
97	
98	`IsEventuallyPeriodic f` in `Rule30/Prize.lean` is `∃ p > 0, ∃ N, PeriodicFrom
99	f p N`, written out; that file keeps the unfolded form so the prize statement
100	reads on its own. Note `p = 0` makes this trivially true, so a statement that
101	means "genuinely periodic" must carry `0 < p` alongside it. -/
102	def PeriodicFrom (f : Nat → Bool) (p N : Nat) : Prop := ∀ n ≥ N, f (n + p) = f n
103	
104	/-- **The bridging lemma.** Rule 30 in closed form: the new cell is the left
105	neighbour XOR (centre OR right neighbour).
106	
107	This is the identity every downstream proof — and the BigInt explorer's
108	`(x <<< 1) ^^^ (x ||| (x >>> 1))` — actually works with. Going from the lookup
109	table to this formula is pure case analysis: `cases` on each of the three
110	Booleans gives 8 goals, and each one is a concrete `Nat.testBit 30 k` that the
111	kernel simply computes. -/
112	theorem rule30_eq (c : Config) (i : ℤ) :
113	    rule30 c i = xor (c (i - 1)) (c i || c (i + 1)) := by
114	  show ElementaryCA.step 30 c i = _
115	  unfold ElementaryCA.step ElementaryCA.neighborhoodIndex
116	  cases c (i - 1) <;> cases c i <;> cases c (i + 1) <;> rfl
117	
118	/-- `evolve` unfolded one step, so that `rule30_eq` can be applied to it. -/
119	theorem evolve_succ (t : Nat) : evolve (t + 1) = rule30 (evolve t) := by
120	  simp [evolve, Function.iterate_succ_apply']
121	
122	/-! ## Arbitrary rows
123	
124	Everything above grows the picture from one black cell. The tools the
125	literature uses on the columns question — left-permutivity, preimage
126	counting — are about *any* starting row, so here the same picture is grown
127	from an arbitrary `c : Config`. `evolve t` is the special case
128	`evolveFrom initialConfig t`, and the two are equal by definition. -/
129	
130	/-- The row after `t` steps of rule 30, starting from any row `c`.
131	
132	The same `f^[t]` iterate as `evolve`, with the starting row a parameter
133	instead of the fixed `initialConfig`. In TypeScript this is the difference
134	between `evolve(t)` and `evolveFrom(c, t)` where the first is
135	`evolveFrom(initialConfig, t)` by definition. -/
136	def evolveFrom (c : Config) (t : Nat) : Config := rule30^[t] c
137

139	after `t` steps, as a function of `t`. `centerColumn` is `column initialConfig 0`. -/
140	def column (c : Config) (i : ℤ) (t : Nat) : Bool := evolveFrom c t i
141	
142	/-- The cells of `c` at positions `-t .. t`, as a function on the finite type
143	`Fin (2 * t + 1)`: index `k` reads position `k - t`.
144	
145	The point of a *finite* type is counting. `Fin n → Bool` has `2 ^ n`
146	inhabitants and Mathlib knows it (`Fintype`), so "all windows of width
147	`2t + 1`" is `Finset.univ` and can be filtered and counted. A `Config` is
148	`ℤ → Bool` and has no such thing. -/
149	def window (c : Config) (t : Nat) : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool :=
150	  fun k => c ((k : ℤ) - (t : ℤ))
151

153	`window (ofWindow w) t = w`, and the picture grown from `ofWindow w` agrees

155	window is `w` (that is the cone lemma, `evolveFrom_eq_of_agree_on_window`). -/
156	def ofWindow {t : Nat} (w : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool) : Config :=
157	  fun i => if h : 0 ≤ i + t ∧ i + t < 2 * t + 1 then w ⟨(i + t).toNat, by omega⟩ else false
158	
159	/-- `f` is **left-permutive** with radius `r`: two rows that agree at every
160	position `i - r + 1 .. i + r` and differ at `i - r` are sent to rows that
161	differ at `i`. Flipping the leftmost cell that a step reads always flips its
162	output, whatever the other cells hold.
163

165	step of rule 30 it is `rule30_eq` read as "`xor` with the left neighbour":

168	def LeftPermutive (f : Config → Config) (r : Nat) : Prop :=
169	  ∀ (c d : Config) (i : ℤ),
170	    (∀ j : ℤ, i - r < j → j ≤ i + r → c j = d j) → c (i - r) ≠ d (i - r) → f c i ≠ f d i
171	
172	/-- How many of the `2 ^ (2t + 1)` windows of width `2t + 1` grow a black
173	centre cell after `t` steps. `window_count_half` says it is exactly half. -/
174	def blackWindowCount (t : Nat) : Nat :=
175	  (Finset.univ.filter fun w : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool =>
176	    evolveFrom (ofWindow w) t 0 = true).card
177

179	theorem evolve_eq_evolveFrom_initial (t : Nat) :
180	    evolve t = evolveFrom initialConfig t := rfl
181

185

187	that `rule30_eq` can be applied to the picture grown from any row. -/
188	theorem evolveFrom_succ (c : Config) (t : Nat) :
189	    evolveFrom c (t + 1) = rule30 (evolveFrom c t) := by
190	  simp [evolveFrom, Function.iterate_succ_apply']

192	/-! ## The row model
193	
194	A row of the single-seed picture has at most `2t + 1` cells, so it fits in
195	one natural number, and one step of rule 30 is three big-integer operations.
196	Lean's kernel evaluates `Nat` arithmetic with built-in bignums, so `decide`
197	can compute row 5000 in a second where evaluating `evolve` cell by cell
198	gives out near row 18. `rowCell_eq_evolve` (a node on the board) says the
199	model and the definition agree; after it, a concrete fact about any row to
200	depth in the thousands is a theorem by `decide`, with no extra axiom. -/
201	
202	/-- Row `t` of the single-seed picture as one number: the cell at position
203	`x` is bit `x + t`, so bit `0` is the left edge and bit `2t` the right edge.
204	
205	The step is `rule30_eq` on all bits at once. `4 * r` shifts the row two bits
206	up so that bit `b` of it is the *left* neighbour of position `b - t - 1`;
207	`2 * r` is the centre; `r` itself is the right neighbour; and
208	`(4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)` is `left XOR (centre OR right)`. The explorer's
209	BigInt engine does the same thing with shifts. -/
210	def rowNat : Nat → Nat
211	  | 0 => 1
212	  | t + 1 => let r := rowNat t; (4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)
213	
214	/-- The cell at position `x` of row `t`, read from `rowNat`; white outside
215	the cone `-t .. t`, where the number has no bit for it. -/
216	def rowCell (t : Nat) (x : ℤ) : Bool :=
217	  if -(t : ℤ) ≤ x ∧ x ≤ t then (rowNat t).testBit (x + t).toNat else false
218	
219	/-- The model agrees with `evolve` on every cell of the first seven rows. A
220	kernel computation, kept in the file as a guard against the orientation
221	error that is easy to make here (the mirror image is rule 86 and passes
222	every symmetric check). The general statement is `rowCell_eq_evolve`. -/
223	example : ∀ t : Fin 7, ∀ x : Fin 13, rowCell t ((x : ℤ) - 6) = evolve t ((x : ℤ) - 6) := by
224	  decide
225	
226	/-! ## The two half-lines and the sideways solve
227	
228	Each half of the picture is driven by the centre column alone. A cell at
229	position `x ≥ 1` reads only positions `x - 1`, `x`, `x + 1`, all `≥ 0`, so
230	the right half `x ≥ 1`, given its own row 0 and the centre column as a
231	boundary, evolves without ever looking left of the origin; the left half is
232	the mirror. And columns 0 and 1 together determine everything to their
233	left, one column per step of `sideways_inverse`. The three definitions below
234	make these views into functions of `ℕ` alone, so they can be stated and
235	computed without a `Config`; the agreement theorems in `Statements.lean`
236	tie each back to `column`.
237	
238	In TypeScript terms, `evolve` is a loop over the whole infinite row, and
239	`evolveHalfLeft c w` is the same loop over a half-open array whose closed
240	end reads `c t` instead of a neighbour. The seam is that the boundary is a
241	*given* sequence here, not something the loop computes — which is exactly
242	why the half-line can be fed a boundary that no row would produce. -/
243	
244	/-- The left half-line: `evolveHalfLeft c w t k` is the cell at position
245	`-(k + 1)` after `t` steps, grown from row 0 `w` (`w k` is the cell at
246	`-(k + 1)`) with the boundary column `c` standing in for position `0`. -/
247	def evolveHalfLeft (c w : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
248	  | 0, k => w k
249	  | t + 1, 0 => xor (evolveHalfLeft c w t 1) (evolveHalfLeft c w t 0 || c t)
250	  | t + 1, k + 1 =>
251	      xor (evolveHalfLeft c w t (k + 2))
252	        (evolveHalfLeft c w t (k + 1) || evolveHalfLeft c w t k)
253	
254	/-- The right half-line: `evolveHalfRight c y t k` is the cell at position
255	`k + 1` after `t` steps, grown from row 0 `y` (`y k` is the cell at `k + 1`)
256	with the boundary column `c` standing in for position `0`. -/
257	def evolveHalfRight (c y : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
258	  | 0, k => y k
259	  | t + 1, 0 => xor (c t) (evolveHalfRight c y t 0 || evolveHalfRight c y t 1)
260	  | t + 1, k + 1 =>
261	      xor (evolveHalfRight c y t k)
262	        (evolveHalfRight c y t (k + 1) || evolveHalfRight c y t (k + 2))
263	
264	/-- The sideways solve: `leftSolve c d k t` is the cell at position `-k` at

269	def leftSolve (c d : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool

271	  | 1, t => xor (c (t + 1)) (c t || d t)
272	  | k + 2, t =>
273	      xor (leftSolve c d (k + 1) (t + 1))

275

279	general statements are `evolveHalfLeft_eq_column`, `evolveHalfRight_eq_column`

# Rule 30 — core definitions

An *elementary cellular automaton* is about as small as a dynamical system
gets: a bi-infinite row of black/white cells, updated in lock-step by a rule
that looks only at each cell and its two neighbours.

import Mathlib.Data.Int.Notation
import Mathlib.Logic.Function.Iterate
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Card
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Pi
import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Card

/-- A configuration of the automaton: a bi-infinite row of cells, each black
(`true`) or white (`false`), indexed by the integers.

In TypeScript terms this is exactly `(i: bigint) => boolean`. There is no
array, no bound, and no "edge of the world" — the row really is the function.
-/
abbrev Config : Type := ℤ → Bool

namespace ElementaryCA

/-- The neighbourhood of a cell, packed into the 3-bit number Wolfram numbers
his rules by: `left` is the high bit (4), `center` the middle bit (2), `right`
the low bit (1). So the all-black neighbourhood `111` is index `7`, and the
all-white one `000` is index `0`.

`Bool.toNat` is the obvious `false ↦ 0`, `true ↦ 1`. -/
def neighborhoodIndex (left center right : Bool) : Nat :=

/-- One step of the elementary cellular automaton with rule number `r`.

neighbourhoods, and the rule must supply one output bit for each — so a rule is

its own bound with it, so `step 300` is not a runtime error, it is unwritable.

`Nat.testBit r.val k` reads bit `k` of the rule number, which is the output for
neighbourhood `k`. -/
def step (r : Fin 256) (c : Config) (i : ℤ) : Bool :=
  r.val.testBit (neighborhoodIndex (c (i - 1)) (c i) (c (i + 1)))

/-- Rule 30, the automaton the Wolfram prizes are about.

"calling `step` with a missing argument" — currying is not opt-in here.) -/
def rule30 : Config → Config := ElementaryCA.step 30

/-- The initial configuration the prize questions are stated against: a single
black cell at the origin on an infinite white background.

whether it holds; the two are different things in Lean, and only the `Bool` can
be stored in a cell. -/
def initialConfig : Config := fun i => decide (i = 0)

/-- The configuration after `t` steps of rule 30, starting from
`initialConfig`.

`f^[t]` is `Nat.iterate`: `f` composed with itself `t` times. `rule30^[0]` is
the identity, so `evolve 0 = initialConfig`. -/
def evolve (t : Nat) : Config := rule30^[t] initialConfig

/-- The center column: the colour of the origin cell after `t` steps.

This single sequence of bits is the subject of all three Rule 30 Prize
questions (see `Rule30/Prize.lean`). It is OEIS A051023. -/
def centerColumn (t : Nat) : Bool := evolve t 0

/-- The `k`-th diagonal in from the **left** edge of the cone, read `j` steps
along it: the cell at position `-j` after `j + k` steps. `leftDiagonal 0` is
the left edge itself, `leftDiagonal 1` the cells just inside it, and so on.

In TypeScript terms it is a re-indexing, `(k, j) => evolve(j + k)(-j)`, and
nothing more — no new data, only a coordinate system in which the left side
of the pattern reads as a family of one-dimensional sequences. -/
def leftDiagonal (k j : Nat) : Bool := evolve (j + k) (-(j : ℤ))

/-- The `k`-th diagonal in from the **right** edge, read `j` steps along it:
the cell at position `j` after `j + k` steps. Not the mirror image of
`leftDiagonal`: rule 30 is not left-right symmetric, and the two families
behave differently. -/
def rightDiagonal (k j : Nat) : Bool := evolve (j + k) (j : ℤ)

/-- `f` repeats with period `p` from index `N` on: `f (n + p) = f n` for every
`n ≥ N`. The prefix before `N` is unconstrained.

`IsEventuallyPeriodic f` in `Rule30/Prize.lean` is `∃ p > 0, ∃ N, PeriodicFrom
f p N`, written out; that file keeps the unfolded form so the prize statement
reads on its own. Note `p = 0` makes this trivially true, so a statement that
means "genuinely periodic" must carry `0 < p` alongside it. -/
def PeriodicFrom (f : Nat → Bool) (p N : Nat) : Prop := ∀ n ≥ N, f (n + p) = f n

/-- **The bridging lemma.** Rule 30 in closed form: the new cell is the left
neighbour XOR (centre OR right neighbour).

This is the identity every downstream proof — and the BigInt explorer's
`(x <<< 1) ^^^ (x ||| (x >>> 1))` — actually works with. Going from the lookup
table to this formula is pure case analysis: `cases` on each of the three
Booleans gives 8 goals, and each one is a concrete `Nat.testBit 30 k` that the
kernel simply computes. -/
theorem rule30_eq (c : Config) (i : ℤ) :
    rule30 c i = xor (c (i - 1)) (c i || c (i + 1)) := by
  show ElementaryCA.step 30 c i = _
  unfold ElementaryCA.step ElementaryCA.neighborhoodIndex
  cases c (i - 1) <;> cases c i <;> cases c (i + 1) <;> rfl

/-- `evolve` unfolded one step, so that `rule30_eq` can be applied to it. -/
theorem evolve_succ (t : Nat) : evolve (t + 1) = rule30 (evolve t) := by
  simp [evolve, Function.iterate_succ_apply']

/-! ## Arbitrary rows

Everything above grows the picture from one black cell. The tools the
literature uses on the columns question — left-permutivity, preimage
counting — are about *any* starting row, so here the same picture is grown
from an arbitrary `c : Config`. `evolve t` is the special case
`evolveFrom initialConfig t`, and the two are equal by definition. -/

/-- The row after `t` steps of rule 30, starting from any row `c`.

The same `f^[t]` iterate as `evolve`, with the starting row a parameter
instead of the fixed `initialConfig`. In TypeScript this is the difference
between `evolve(t)` and `evolveFrom(c, t)` where the first is
`evolveFrom(initialConfig, t)` by definition. -/
def evolveFrom (c : Config) (t : Nat) : Config := rule30^[t] c

/-- Column `i` of the picture grown from `c`: the colour of position `i`
after `t` steps, as a function of `t`. `centerColumn` is `column initialConfig 0`. -/
def column (c : Config) (i : ℤ) (t : Nat) : Bool := evolveFrom c t i

/-- The cells of `c` at positions `-t .. t`, as a function on the finite type
`Fin (2 * t + 1)`: index `k` reads position `k - t`.

The point of a *finite* type is counting. `Fin n → Bool` has `2 ^ n`
inhabitants and Mathlib knows it (`Fintype`), so "all windows of width
`2t + 1`" is `Finset.univ` and can be filtered and counted. A `Config` is
`ℤ → Bool` and has no such thing. -/
def window (c : Config) (t : Nat) : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool :=
  fun k => c ((k : ℤ) - (t : ℤ))

/-- A window extended by white cells outside `-t .. t`, back to a full row.
`window (ofWindow w) t = w`, and the picture grown from `ofWindow w` agrees
at the origin for `t` steps with the picture grown from any row whose
window is `w` (that is the cone lemma, `evolveFrom_eq_of_agree_on_window`). -/
def ofWindow {t : Nat} (w : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool) : Config :=
  fun i => if h : 0 ≤ i + t ∧ i + t < 2 * t + 1 then w ⟨(i + t).toNat, by omega⟩ else false

/-- `f` is **left-permutive** with radius `r`: two rows that agree at every
position `i - r + 1 .. i + r` and differ at `i - r` are sent to rows that
differ at `i`. Flipping the leftmost cell that a step reads always flips its
output, whatever the other cells hold.

This is the property everything about rule 30's columns leans on. For one
step of rule 30 it is `rule30_eq` read as "`xor` with the left neighbour":
`rule30_leftPermutive`. For `t` steps it is `evolveFrom_leftPermutive`, with
radius `t`. -/
def LeftPermutive (f : Config → Config) (r : Nat) : Prop :=
  ∀ (c d : Config) (i : ℤ),
    (∀ j : ℤ, i - r < j → j ≤ i + r → c j = d j) → c (i - r) ≠ d (i - r) → f c i ≠ f d i

/-- How many of the `2 ^ (2t + 1)` windows of width `2t + 1` grow a black
centre cell after `t` steps. `window_count_half` says it is exactly half. -/
def blackWindowCount (t : Nat) : Nat :=
  (Finset.univ.filter fun w : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool =>
    evolveFrom (ofWindow w) t 0 = true).card

/-- The single-seed picture is the general one grown from `initialConfig`. -/
theorem evolve_eq_evolveFrom_initial (t : Nat) :
    evolve t = evolveFrom initialConfig t := rfl

/-- The centre column is column `0` of the single-seed picture. -/
theorem centerColumn_eq_column (t : Nat) :
    centerColumn t = column initialConfig 0 t := rfl

/-- `evolveFrom` unfolded one step, the way `evolve_succ` unfolds `evolve`, so
that `rule30_eq` can be applied to the picture grown from any row. -/
theorem evolveFrom_succ (c : Config) (t : Nat) :
    evolveFrom c (t + 1) = rule30 (evolveFrom c t) := by
  simp [evolveFrom, Function.iterate_succ_apply']

/-! ## The row model

A row of the single-seed picture has at most `2t + 1` cells, so it fits in
one natural number, and one step of rule 30 is three big-integer operations.
Lean's kernel evaluates `Nat` arithmetic with built-in bignums, so `decide`
can compute row 5000 in a second where evaluating `evolve` cell by cell
gives out near row 18. `rowCell_eq_evolve` (a node on the board) says the
model and the definition agree; after it, a concrete fact about any row to
depth in the thousands is a theorem by `decide`, with no extra axiom. -/

/-- Row `t` of the single-seed picture as one number: the cell at position
`x` is bit `x + t`, so bit `0` is the left edge and bit `2t` the right edge.

The step is `rule30_eq` on all bits at once. `4 * r` shifts the row two bits
up so that bit `b` of it is the *left* neighbour of position `b - t - 1`;
`2 * r` is the centre; `r` itself is the right neighbour; and
`(4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)` is `left XOR (centre OR right)`. The explorer's
BigInt engine does the same thing with shifts. -/
def rowNat : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 1
  | t + 1 => let r := rowNat t; (4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)

/-- The cell at position `x` of row `t`, read from `rowNat`; white outside
the cone `-t .. t`, where the number has no bit for it. -/
def rowCell (t : Nat) (x : ℤ) : Bool :=
  if -(t : ℤ) ≤ x ∧ x ≤ t then (rowNat t).testBit (x + t).toNat else false

/-- The model agrees with `evolve` on every cell of the first seven rows. A
kernel computation, kept in the file as a guard against the orientation
error that is easy to make here (the mirror image is rule 86 and passes
every symmetric check). The general statement is `rowCell_eq_evolve`. -/
example : ∀ t : Fin 7, ∀ x : Fin 13, rowCell t ((x : ℤ) - 6) = evolve t ((x : ℤ) - 6) := by
  decide

/-! ## The two half-lines and the sideways solve

Each half of the picture is driven by the centre column alone. A cell at
position `x ≥ 1` reads only positions `x - 1`, `x`, `x + 1`, all `≥ 0`, so
the right half `x ≥ 1`, given its own row 0 and the centre column as a
boundary, evolves without ever looking left of the origin; the left half is
the mirror. And columns 0 and 1 together determine everything to their
left, one column per step of `sideways_inverse`. The three definitions below
make these views into functions of `ℕ` alone, so they can be stated and
computed without a `Config`; the agreement theorems in `Statements.lean`
tie each back to `column`.

In TypeScript terms, `evolve` is a loop over the whole infinite row, and
`evolveHalfLeft c w` is the same loop over a half-open array whose closed
end reads `c t` instead of a neighbour. The seam is that the boundary is a
*given* sequence here, not something the loop computes — which is exactly
why the half-line can be fed a boundary that no row would produce. -/

/-- The left half-line: `evolveHalfLeft c w t k` is the cell at position
`-(k + 1)` after `t` steps, grown from row 0 `w` (`w k` is the cell at
`-(k + 1)`) with the boundary column `c` standing in for position `0`. -/
def evolveHalfLeft (c w : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
  | 0, k => w k
  | t + 1, 0 => xor (evolveHalfLeft c w t 1) (evolveHalfLeft c w t 0 || c t)
  | t + 1, k + 1 =>
      xor (evolveHalfLeft c w t (k + 2))
        (evolveHalfLeft c w t (k + 1) || evolveHalfLeft c w t k)

/-- The right half-line: `evolveHalfRight c y t k` is the cell at position
`k + 1` after `t` steps, grown from row 0 `y` (`y k` is the cell at `k + 1`)
with the boundary column `c` standing in for position `0`. -/
def evolveHalfRight (c y : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
  | 0, k => y k
  | t + 1, 0 => xor (c t) (evolveHalfRight c y t 0 || evolveHalfRight c y t 1)
  | t + 1, k + 1 =>
      xor (evolveHalfRight c y t k)
        (evolveHalfRight c y t (k + 1) || evolveHalfRight c y t (k + 2))

/-- The sideways solve: `leftSolve c d k t` is the cell at position `-k` at
time `t`, rebuilt from column `0` (`c`) and column `1` (`d`) alone by
`sideways_inverse`, one column per step leftward: the cell at `-(k + 1)` is
the cell at `-k` one step later, XOR (the cell at `-k` OR the cell at
`-k + 1`). Column `1` is read only in the first step. -/
def leftSolve (c d : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
  | 0, t => c t
  | 1, t => xor (c (t + 1)) (c t || d t)
  | k + 2, t =>
      xor (leftSolve c d (k + 1) (t + 1))
        (leftSolve c d (k + 1) t || leftSolve c d k t)

/-- The three models agree with the row model on the single seed for the
first steps. Kernel computations kept in the file as guards against an
orientation error (a mirrored half-line passes every symmetric check); the
general statements are `evolveHalfLeft_eq_column`, `evolveHalfRight_eq_column`
and `leftSolve_eq_column`. -/
example : ∀ t : Fin 8, ∀ k : Fin 8,
    evolveHalfLeft (fun t => rowCell t 0) (fun _ => false) t k
      = rowCell t (-((k : ℤ) + 1)) := by
  decide

example : ∀ t : Fin 8, ∀ k : Fin 8,
    evolveHalfRight (fun t => rowCell t 0) (fun _ => false) t k
      = rowCell t ((k : ℤ) + 1) := by
  decide

example : ∀ k : Fin 7, ∀ t : Fin 7,
    leftSolve (fun t => rowCell t 0) (fun t => rowCell t 1) k t
      = rowCell t (-(k : ℤ)) := by
  decide
